title: Caesar salad
summary: Crisp romaine in an egg-yolk, lemon and garlic dressing seasoned with anchovy, Worcestershire and parmesan, scattered with almond-flour crisps in place of croutons.

ingredients.note: pasteurised if serving the young, elderly or pregnant
optional; leave out for a milder dressing
two large hearts, torn or chopped

steps: Heat the oven to 165 °C (325 °F) and line a baking sheet with parchment. Mix the almond flour, egg white, olive oil, garlic powder and salt into a stiff paste. Spread it thinly, about 3 mm (1/8 in), on the parchment and bake 10–12 minutes, until golden. Cool, then break into crouton-size pieces.

Mash the anchovies and garlic to a paste with the side of a knife, then whisk them in a bowl with the egg yolk, lemon juice, Worcestershire and mustard. Whisk in the olive oil a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream, until thick and glossy. Stir in half the parmesan and the pepper. Thin with a teaspoon of water if needed.
Toss the romaine with the dressing until every leaf is coated. Top with the crisps and the remaining parmesan and serve at once.
dairy_free_notes: Nutritional yeast gives the dressing a savoury, nutty depth but not parmesan's saltiness; add a pinch of salt and another dash of Worcestershire.
tips: Anchovies and Worcestershire both contain fish. Without the anchovies the dressing is milder, and Worcestershire still gives it some savoury depth; Cardini's original is said to have used Worcestershire alone.
The crisps keep a week in an airtight jar.

origin.history: The salad is usually credited to Caesar Cardini, an Italian-born restaurateur who ran a restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico, in the 1920s and is said to have improvised it from what was in his kitchen; the exact year and the details of the story vary, and other people have claimed it. Cardini's own version reportedly relied on Worcestershire sauce rather than whole anchovies.
